fixes.explanation: Armor never comes up in Saul's oath. Saul, Israel's king, cursed the man who eats any food before evening (1 Samuel 14:24). The oath was about food, nothing else. Nothing in it touches their equipment.

Jonathan, Saul's son, did not walk past. He had not heard that his father had bound the people with the oath. So he reached out the end of his staff, dipped it into the honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth (1 Samuel 14:27). The troops left the honey alone, but Jonathan didn't.

Right, he didn't leave it alone. Jonathan, Saul's son, had not heard about the oath, so he dipped the end of his staff into the honeycomb and put his hand to his mouth (1 Samuel 14:27). And his eyes brightened. The troops around him wouldn't touch the honey because they feared the oath (1 Samuel 14:26).

Scattered isn't the word the soldier uses. He tells Jonathan, Saul's son, that the oath is why “…the people are faint.” (1 Samuel 14:28). The word is about their strength running low. It's not about where they were.

Saul built an altar to the LORD. The text adds that it was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD (1 Samuel 14:35). The troops had just slaughtered their oxen there (1 Samuel 14:34). That's a first worth noticing.
No tower here. The text says Saul built an altar to the LORD (1 Samuel 14:35). It was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD. A tower would have taken me a whole lot longer to stamp.

No storehouse, friend. The text says Saul built an altar to the LORD, and it was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD (1 Samuel 14:35). Saul had told the troops to bring their oxen and sheep and slaughter them in that place (1 Samuel 14:34). An altar is what went up.

Not this time. Saul asked God whether he should go down after the Philistines, “But God did not answer him that day.” (1 Samuel 14:37). Saul asked and got no answer. Then Saul called the leaders together to investigate how this sin had occurred (1 Samuel 14:38).

Saul says, “As surely as the LORD who saves Israel lives, even if it is my son Jonathan, he must die!” (1 Samuel 14:39). Jonathan is Saul's son, and Saul names him before the lot is cast. The lot comes later, in verses 41 and 42. That's a big promise to make so early.

Ishvi is one of Saul's sons (1 Samuel 14:49), but he isn't the one Saul names in his oath. Saul says, “…even if it is my son Jonathan, he must die!” (1 Samuel 14:39). Jonathan is the name in the oath. Ishvi shows up only in the list of Saul's family.
Banished isn't the word. The text says, “So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.” (1 Samuel 14:45). The people stepped in for him. Rescued is the word the text uses.
